sections.explanation: Factorisation reverses distribution: identify a factor multiplying every term and put it outside brackets. Cancellation is division of the whole numerator and denominator by a common non-zero factor. It does not remove selected terms from a sum. An excluded input remains excluded after simplification, even if the simplified formula happens to have a value there. Retain that restriction alongside your answer.
sections.worked: (6x + 9)/3 = 3(2x + 3)/3 = 2x + 3. In contrast, (x² + 3x)/x = x(x + 3)/x = x + 3 only for x ≠ 0. The original fraction does not acquire a value at zero through cancellation.

feedback: At x = 2 the original is 2, so that test happens to agree; at x = 1 it is 3, disproving the general claim. Only factors cancel.

sections.explanation: To add algebraic fractions, use a common denominator exactly as with numerical fractions. Multiply the numerator as well as the denominator when changing a fraction’s form. State restrictions from the original denominators first. For products, factor before cancelling. A numerator becoming zero is usually allowed; a denominator becoming zero is not. Keep these different cases separate.
sections.worked: 1/x + 2/(3x) = 3/(3x) + 2/(3x) = 5/(3x), x ≠ 0. Also (2x + 4)/(x + 2) = 2(x + 2)/(x + 2) = 2 for x ≠ −2. The restriction survives even though the final expression looks constant.

sections.explanation: ZeroDivisionError reports an attempted division by zero. It identifies an invalid arithmetic operation, not an instruction to ignore the restriction. First evaluate both forms at permitted inputs. Then deliberately try an excluded value in a separate cell, read the last line of the error, and explain it. Remove or comment out that deliberate error before your final clean run. A comment starts with # and is ignored by Python.
sections.worked: For (x² + 3x)/x and x + 3, x = 2 gives 5 in both forms. With x = 0 the original raises ZeroDivisionError, while the simplified expression alone gives 3. That difference is why the domain is part of the equivalence statement.

sections.explanation: Average speed in a supplied constant-speed model is distance divided by elapsed time. If distance is written vt, then vt/t = v for t ≠ 0. In the physical interval model we normally require t > 0 as well. An algebraic restriction and a physical restriction can differ: negative time intervals may be allowed algebraically but excluded by the meaning of a particular experiment.
sections.worked: At v = 4 m/s and t = 3 s, distance is 12 m and distance/time is 4 m/s. At t = 0, the quotient is 0/0 and undefined. The simplified symbol v does not make that quotient defined.

sections.explanation: A useful simplification record contains the original expression, the factored form, the final expression and the original restrictions. Use a fresh numerical input to catch errors, then identify the algebraic law that justifies each step. If cancellation is tempting, point to the common factor of the whole numerator and denominator before doing it.
sections.worked: (5x − 10)/(x − 2) = 5(x − 2)/(x − 2) = 5, x ≠ 2. A check at x = 3 gives 5, but the written factorisation is the justification.
